# Feature Specification: genproj "Container Agent" Capability

**Status**: Implemented
**Created**: 2026-09-17
**Motivating use case**: every generated devcontainer should be reachable as an agent. A repo generated by genproj gets goose, MCP servers and recipes inside its container (`coding-agents`), but nothing outside the container can talk to it: there is no card, no registry entry, no stable name. Peers on the tailnet — the LiteLLM proxy, other containers, a host — can only reach a container that has published a card.
**Depends on**: `coding-agents` (the agent drives the goose in that container). The tailnet wiring is provided unconditionally by the devcontainer generator, so there is no separate capability for it.
**Reference implementation**: `specs/007-genproj-github-release/spec.md` — the release channel this capability consumes.

---

## 1. Problem

The generator produces containers that host an agent but do not **register** one. Closing that gap by hand, per repo, is what the `container-agent` capability exists to remove.

The shape of the problem is worth stating, because it decides the design:

- **The agent cannot be baked into the image.** It ships as a GitHub Release and is installed by a launcher that self-updates (`a2a-goose`'s `fetch-launch.sh`), exactly like a host. Using the same channel means a container and a host run the same code by construction, and a fix ships the same way to both.
- **The card's public URL must not be loopback.** The agent refuses to start on one, because a loopback address is wrong for the only reader that matters: LiteLLM, on another machine. The address has to be the container's tailnet name.
- **A container is stopped, not shut down.** An agent that is SIGKILLed leaves a stale registry row; one that is SIGTERMed deregisters. The gap between those two is a docker-run flag, not application code.
- **A devcontainer must come up without an agent.** If the network is not there on a first start, the project is still the point. The agent is not allowed to make the container unusable.

## 2. Capability definition

Machine-readable contract: `contracts/container-agent.capability.json`. Summary:

| field                 | value                                                                                                               |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `id`                  | `container-agent`                                                                                                   |
| `category`            | `core` — it is part of every container, not an optional extra                                                       |
| `locked`              | `true` — a client must not offer to deselect it                                                                     |
| `selectedByDefault`   | `true`                                                                                                              |
| `dependencies`        | `["coding-agents"]`                                                                                                 |
| `conflicts`           | `[]`                                                                                                                |
| `requiresAuth`        | `[]`                                                                                                                |
| `authServices`        | `[]` — secrets come from Doppler at start time, so nothing is provisioned at generation time                        |
| `externalServices`    | `[]` — the release channel is consumed by the container, not by the generator                                       |
| `configurationSchema` | `litellmBaseUrl` (`http://nas:4000`), `nameSuffix` (`-dev`), `tailnetName` (`""` → derived from `tailscale status`) |

### 2.1 It is not droppable, and not only in the UI

`selectedByDefault` is a default: a client may turn it off. That is the wrong semantic for a container agent, so the dependency is expressed where a client cannot route around it — **every `devcontainer-*` capability declares `container-agent` as a dependency**:

```
devcontainer-node   → ["docker", "container-agent"]
devcontainer-python → ["docker", "container-agent"]
devcontainer-java   → ["docker", "container-agent"]
devcontainer-rust   → ["docker", "container-agent"]
```

Selecting a devcontainer therefore _is_ selecting its agent, for the API and MCP callers as much as for the UI. `locked: true` is the separate, weaker thing the UI needs: the signal to render the capability as present-but-not-deselectable rather than as a suggestion.

This required a fix in the resolver: `resolveDependencies` added only one level of dependencies, so the chain `devcontainer-* → container-agent → coding-agents` would have silently dropped `coding-agents`. It is now a cycle-safe worklist closure, preserving the existing `{ resolvedCapabilities, addedDependencies, conflicts, isValid }` shape. That bug was latent before this capability; this is the first chain long enough to expose it.

### 2.2 What the capability emits

| Path                                | Owned by | Purpose                                                                                       |
| ----------------------------------- | -------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `scripts/agent-dev.sh`              | app      | `start` / `stop` / `status` for this container's agent; seeded once, never overwritten        |
| `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json`   | genproj  | `--stop-timeout 30` appended to `runArgs`                                                     |
| `.devcontainer/post-start-setup.sh` | genproj  | runs `scripts/agent-dev.sh start` on every container start, guarded so the script is optional |
| `README.md`                         | genproj  | names the agent and documents the three subcommands                                           |

`scripts/` is app-owned, so `agent-dev.sh` is seeded once and then belongs to the project — the same rule as `release-artifacts.sh` (007 §2). That matters more here than there: the script is the only thing in the repo that knows the container's own agent name, and a project that needs to diverge (a different ACP URL, an extra env var) must be able to without a regeneration undoing it.

## 3. Flow: how the agent comes up

```
devcontainer start
        │
        ▼
post-start-setup.sh ──► scripts/agent-dev.sh start            (idempotent, fails open)
        │
        ├─ resolve the tailnet name   tailnetName config, else `tailscale status --json`
        │                             (fail loudly rather than write a loopback publicUrl)
        ├─ write ~/.config/a2a-goose/env      0600, secrets from Doppler (own config, else common), never containerEnv
        ├─ write ~/.config/a2a-goose/config.yaml
        │       card.name / registry.agentName = <repo><nameSuffix>
        │       server.bind 0.0.0.0:10001, server.publicUrl http://<tailnetName>:10001
        │       goose.acp.url http://127.0.0.1:3284/acp, goose.defaults.cwd /workspaces/<repo>
        ├─ ensure the launcher        cold start only: curl releases/latest/download/fetch-launch.sh
        └─ run it backgrounded        output to ~/.local/state/a2a-goose/agent.log, pid file beside it

docker stop ──► SIGTERM ──► deregister ──► goose child exits (~8s measured) ──► --stop-timeout 30 is headroom
```

**Fail open is the first rule.** A first start with no network prints why the agent did not start and exits 0. The devcontainer comes up either way — including the case the hook is designed around, where the container is starting for the first time on a machine that has never fetched the launcher.

**One agent per repo is the contract.** The registry row is keyed by name (`<repo><nameSuffix>`), so a start _reclaims_ the row a previous container left behind rather than adding a second agent. A clean stop deregisters; an unclean death leaves a row that the next start overwrites by name.

### 3.1 Why `--stop-timeout` is a devcontainer change

`devcontainer.json` has no `stop_grace_period` key — that is a compose-only setting. For a `docker run`-based container the equivalent is docker's own `--stop-timeout`, which the devcontainer CLI passes through `runArgs`. The measured goose child shutdown is ~8s; 30s is headroom, so nobody waits on it.

### 3.2 Why post-start, not post-create

`post-create` runs once, at build time. `post-start` runs on every start and resume. An agent registered in `post-create` is absent for every session that did not rebuild the container — which is nearly all of them. The hook is in post-start because being present is the whole feature.

### 3.3 Where the secrets come from, and why that is not `authServices`

`authServices` is empty and stays empty: nothing is provisioned at generation time, so there is no service for the generator to authorise against. The agent reads four values at start time instead, and writes them to `~/.config/a2a-goose/env` (mode 0600, sourced by the launcher with `set -a`, never in `containerEnv`, never on a command line):

| key                        | why the agent needs it                                           |
| -------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `A2A_GOOSE_BEARER_TOKEN`   | the card's bearer token — a2a-goose refuses to start without one |
| `GOOSE_SERVER__SECRET_KEY` | handed to the goose child as its `X-Secret-Key`                  |
| `LITELLM_MASTER_KEY`       | registry authentication                                          |
| `LITELLM_BASE_URL`         | the registry address                                             |

Each is looked up in the repo's **own** Doppler config first — so a repo that wants its own token keeps it — and then in the shared `common` project (`common/prd`, overridable with `A2A_GOOSE_COMMON_PROJECT` / `A2A_GOOSE_COMMON_CONFIG`). The fallback is the point: these are per-agent-installation values that every container needs the same copy of, and the alternative is putting them in each repo's config and re-provisioning all of them when one rotates. `LITELLM_BASE_URL` is the one duplicate of the capability's own `litellmBaseUrl`; the config file's value is what the agent dials, and the env copy exists only so the env file is complete.

A start with no `A2A_GOOSE_BEARER_TOKEN` is **not** attempted. a2a-goose refuses to start without it, so launching anyway would turn a knowable "no token" into a refusal buried in a log; `write_env_file` says the reason once and cmd_start returns. Fail-open still holds — exit 0, the container is untouched — but the message is the reason rather than a preamble to one.

## 4. Backport: what lets an existing container gain an agent

The capability reaches repos that already exist through the same machinery, which is why two merge properties had to be true:

- **`devcontainer.json` is a merge target** (additive, monotonic). `--stop-timeout` reaches an existing devcontainer because `mergeDevcontainerJson` now **unions `runArgs`** — existing entries first, generated-only additions appended, deduped. Before this, `runArgs` was in the "keep existing values" bucket, so the flag would have been generated and then silently discarded for every repo that already had a devcontainer, which is all of them.
- **`scripts/` is app-owned.** `scripts/agent-dev.sh` is seeded once, on the first regeneration, and never clobbered afterwards (it is deliberately _not_ added to `GENPROJ_OWNED_SCRIPTS`).

So a backport is: add `container-agent` to the repo's selection, regenerate, and the devcontainer bits are added and the script is seeded. Nothing else in the repo moves.

## 5. Acceptance

- [ ] `container-agent` is returned for any selection containing a `devcontainer-*`, including via the API/MCP with no UI in the path, and selecting a devcontainer plus `container-agent` does not double it.
- [ ] `resolveDependencies(["devcontainer-rust"])` contains `docker`, `container-agent` **and** `coding-agents`.
- [ ] The emitted `scripts/agent-dev.sh` has no unresolved `{{...}}` and passes `bash -n`.
- [ ] `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json` has `--stop-timeout 30` in `runArgs`; a project without the capability does not.
- [ ] `.devcontainer/post-start-setup.sh` starts the agent when the capability is selected, and mentions no agent when it is not.
- [ ] The card carries its turn deadline (`turn-deadline/v1`), appears in `list_agents` with its own ceiling read from the agent rather than the row, and a turn through LiteLLM at `/a2a/{agent_id}` gets an answer.
- [ ] `docker stop` → the agent is gone from the roster; a restart reclaims the same row rather than adding one.
- [ ] A first start with no network leaves the devcontainer usable, says why the agent did not start, and exits 0.
- [ ] Merging the freshly generated `devcontainer.json` into an existing one is a no-op the second time, and adds `--stop-timeout` the first.

## 6. Not in v1

- **A `container-tailnet` capability.** The tailnet wiring is unconditional in the devcontainer generator (state volume, `runArgs` sysctls, post-create install, post-start `tailscaled`), so it already _is_ the provider; making it a capability would be a refactor of every devcontainer for no behavioural gain. Container-agent therefore depends only on `coding-agents`.
- **Declaring the card port in `forwardPorts`.** The card is reached over the tailnet. A host port forward is not the path, and declaring one would invite the terminal-scraped forwarding the port-forwarding work exists to stop.
- **Baking the payload into the image.** The release channel is the point (§1).
- **More than one agent per repo.** The registry is keyed by name.
